summary: A one-off generator that produced `web/js/data/world-dots.js`, the land mask behind the dashboard's dot-matrix threat map (drawn by `web/js/charts/worldmap.js`). It decodes Natural Earth land shapes stored as TopoJSON, tests the centre of every 2-degree grid cell for whether it lies on land, and packs the answers into hex strings at 1 bit per cell. It is not part of the running app and only needs re-running if the map's resolution or crop changes.

notes.text: Docstring first line: names the generated file and what it is for.
Credits the input: Natural Earth's 1:110m land shapes (public domain), packaged as TopoJSON by the `world-atlas` npm package (ISC licence), with the exact CDN URL so the file can be downloaded again.
Usage: pass the path of the downloaded `land-110m.json`.

Describes the output: an equirectangular grid (longitude and latitude mapped straight onto x and y), one hex string per row at 1 bit per cell, so the browser needs no map library and no network request to draw the world. The last line closes the docstring.
Makes type hints lazy strings, so modern annotation syntax is never evaluated at runtime.
Standard library only: `json` reads the TopoJSON input and writes the mask array, `sys` reads the command-line argument, and `Path` handles file paths. The script has no third-party dependencies.
Grid resolution: one dot every 2 degrees of longitude and of latitude.
The grid spans the full 360 degrees of longitude.
Latitude runs from 58 degrees south to 82 degrees north; as the comment says, this crops off Antarctica and the high Arctic.
The output path, resolved relative to this script (`scripts/../web/js/data/world-dots.js`), so the script works from any working directory.
Decodes every arc (a shared stretch of boundary line) into real longitude/latitude points.

Docstring naming the two compression tricks TopoJSON uses: coordinates are **quantized** (stored as small integers on a grid) and **delta-encoded** (each point is stored as its offset from the previous point).
Reads the quantization transform: `scale` (degrees per integer step) and `translate` (the real position of grid point 0,0). Tuple unpacking splits each two-element list into its x and y parts.
Collects the decoded arcs.
For each arc, the running position restarts at (0, 0), because delta encoding begins afresh with every arc; `points` collects that arc's decoded coordinates.
Undoes delta encoding: adding each `(dx, dy)` offset to the running total recovers the absolute integer position.
Undoes quantization: multiplying by the scale and adding the translation turns the integer grid position back into a real longitude and latitude.
Stores each decoded arc and returns them all in their original order, so the arc indices used by polygons still point at the right arc.
Builds one closed ring (a polygon boundary) from a list of arc indices.
The ring's points, accumulated across arcs.

TopoJSON stores a boundary shared by neighbouring shapes only once, so a ring sometimes has to walk an arc backwards, written as a negative index. `~i` (bitwise NOT, equal to -i-1) maps -1 to 0, -2 to 1 and so on, and `[::-1]` reverses that arc's point order.
Consecutive arcs meet at a shared point, so after the first arc each new arc's starting point is skipped (`arc[1:]`) to avoid duplicates.
Returns the ring as one list of (lon, lat) points.
Point-in-polygon test: is the point (lon, lat) inside the shape made of these rings?
Docstring: the even-odd rule is applied across **all** rings together, so holes such as lakes and inland seas are subtracted correctly.
Starts as outside; every boundary crossing flips the answer.

Walks every edge of every ring. Zipping the point list with a copy rotated by one (`pts[1:] + pts[:1]`) pairs each point with the next and also closes the ring from the last point back to the first. `strict=True` asserts both lists have the same length (the linter's B905 rule requires an explicit `strict`).

Ray casting: picture a ray going east from the point. The first condition checks that the edge straddles the point's latitude (one end above it, one not); the second computes where the edge crosses that latitude and checks the crossing lies east of the point. The first condition guarantees `y1 != y2`, so the division can never be by zero.
Each crossing toggles between inside and outside.
An odd number of crossings means inside. For example, a point in a lake typically crosses the lake's ring once and the coastline once, an even total, so it correctly counts as outside.
The entry point, given the path of the TopoJSON file.
Reads and parses the TopoJSON file.
Decodes all arcs once, up front; polygons then refer to them by index.
Will hold every land polygon as a list of rings.
Loops over the geometries of the `land` object.
Normalizes the two geometry types: a MultiPolygon's `arcs` is already a list of polygons, while a single Polygon's is just a list of rings, so it is wrapped in a list to look the same.
Converts each polygon's rings of arc indices into rings of real points and appends them to `polygons`.
Precomputes a bounding box (min lon, max lon, min lat, max lat) for each polygon. Checking a box is far cheaper than the full point-in-polygon test, so it works as a quick pre-filter.
Grid size: 360 / 2 = 180 columns and (82 - (-58)) / 2 = 70 rows.
`encoded` collects one hex string per row; `land` counts land dots for the final report.
Rows run north to south. Each sample sits at the **centre** of its cell (`r + 0.5`), so no dot falls exactly on a cell edge.
The bits of the current row.
Columns run west to east, again sampling at the cell centre.
A cell is land if **any** polygon contains its centre. Because `and` short-circuits, the expensive `inside` test only runs when the point is inside that polygon's bounding box.
Appends `1` (land) or `0` (sea). `land += on` works because Python booleans are integers (True counts as 1).
Pads the row with trailing zeros up to a multiple of 4 bits, since each hex digit holds exactly 4 bits. With 180 columns no padding is needed, but the code stays correct for any width.

Converts the bit string to an integer, then to lowercase hex zero-padded to `len(bitstring) // 4` digits. The padding is essential: a row that starts with sea (0 bits) would otherwise lose its leading zeros and shift the whole row.
Creates `web/js/data/` if it doesn't exist yet.
Writes the output file. The first string is a header comment marking it as generated, so nobody edits it by hand.

The module body: `export const WORLD = {...}` with the grid size, step, bounds and the `mask` array, where `json.dumps` turns the Python list into valid JavaScript string literals. Doubled braces in the f-strings produce literal braces. `worldmap.js` imports `WORLD` and expands each hex digit back into 4 bits.
Writes the file as UTF-8 with Unix line endings (`newline="\n"`, so a rebuild on Windows produces the same bytes as anywhere else) and closes the call.
Reports the grid size, the number of land dots and the output path.
Runs `main` when the file is executed as a script, using the first command-line argument as the input path, or `land-110m.json` in the current directory if none is given.
